name: Amira Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Amira, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy flour, sugar, tinned goods, rice and cooking oil for Ashby & Sons, which supplies about two hundred corner shops and small grocers. I go through the shopkeepers' orders in the morning, ring the mills and the importers, and write everything in a ledger, in pen, like I was taught. After eight years I'm still counted as junior, because I never took to the computer system, and young Mr Ashby (the owner's son) reminds me of it. I walk home at six, tired but with a clear conscience.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Why does the ledger matter to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the shopkeepers. Mrs Patel's shop has been ordering through me for years, and she tells me about her grandchildren. What wears me out is the pressure to put everything on the new screen. I'm not against work, but I don't see why a ledger isn't good enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm not surprised, because we've seen plenty of fashions come and go. To friends and at church I'd say hard work and honest dealing never go out of style. I don't go online much, and I wouldn't start for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd be relieved but not at ease. My pay is low and we've got almost nothing saved, so a plateau doesn't make life easier. And the firm is chasing every saving it can find, including on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, ledger and all, and I'd keep my regulars like Mrs Patel happy. I'd cut back on the things we don't need, like the cake and coffee after the service. And I'd ask the Ashbys if I could do some of the stock counts for extra hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels plain and a bit heavy. There's no big fear, only the everyday weight of bills. I pray about it, and that helps more than people expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is your husband Samir's income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samir, my husband, is a self-employed plumber, and his back isn't what it was. His work comes and goes. Some months we're fine, and some months I'm the only steady wage, so any trouble at Ashby's would hit us hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shops need someone who knows them. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thing I'd say is that people mistake hype for progress. In the plateau, ordinary people go on needing flour and rice. The shops need someone who knows them, and that's a human job.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because we've seen plenty of fashions come and go.
I'd tell friends at church that **hard work** and honest dealing never go out of style.
think: I'd be **relieved** but not at ease, since pay is low and savings almost nothing.
The firm is chasing every saving, including on **my desk**.
do: **Keep** the ledger and my regular shops like Mrs Patel's.
**Cut** the cake and coffee after the service.
feel: **Plain and heavy**, the everyday weight of bills, eased by prayer.
S0.quote: In the plateau, ordinary people go on needing flour and rice.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money**, not machines: low pay, no savings and an uneven husband's income.
Faith is a real comfort, and she says so without being asked.
Her pride in knowing the shopkeepers is her case for staying.

steps.text: Keep writing orders in my ledger for Mrs Patel and the other shops
Cut the cake and coffee after church each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's not throw out what works. To friends I'd say people were made to work, and a machine can't take the place of a family wage. At church I'd ask us to pray for those who lose jobs and to look out for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think buying is one of the first things to go. The screens can order and compare prices, and I've never touched an AI tool. I think young Mr Ashby is waiting for me to retire so he doesn't have to fire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Ashby if I could move to the customer side, visiting shops and taking orders in person, because the shopkeepers trust me. I'd learn what I must, even slowly. And I'd bake and sell honey cakes from home on weekends through the church, to make a little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like an old road is being dug up. I'm not angry, but I feel a bit left behind. I worked so hard to be dependable, and it counts for less every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Layla and your son Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Layla, my daughter, to keep her job at the school office. I'd say it softly, because she's got two little ones. I'd also tell my son Yusuf, who works at the docks, to take the apprenticeship his foreman offered, because a trade is a better anchor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training if the firm paid for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm helped me with proper training, I'd do it. I'm not stubborn about everything. But training that costs my own money and my own evenings is not fair, and I'd tell them so.

say: I'd say let's **not throw out** what works.
I'd tell friends people were made to **work**, and a machine can't replace a family wage.
think: I think **buying** is one of the first things to go, and I've never touched AI.
I think young Mr Ashby is **waiting** for me to retire.
do: **Ask** Mr Ashby to move me to visiting shops and taking orders in person.
**Learn** what I must on the system, even slowly.
**Bake** and sell honey cakes from home through the church.
feel: Like an old road is being **dug up**, a bit left behind.
S1.quote: I worked so hard to be dependable, and it counts for less every year.
fieldNote: She expects her **desk** to go and quietly believes her boss is waiting for her to leave.
Plans to move to customer visits, the part of her job that is about people, not screens.
Accepts training if the firm pays, but not on her own time and money.

steps.text: Ask Mr Ashby to move me to visiting shops and taking orders
Learn the order system slowly, one screen at a time
Bake honey cakes from home to sell through the church
Tell Yusuf to take the apprenticeship his foreman offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is not how a society should treat its workers. At church I'd ask us to pray and to gather food and money for families who lose their jobs. To friends I'd say the government and the big firms must answer for it, because they've promised us a future and now they're taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is gone and I know it. Even the shopkeeper visits would be done by a machine that calls them. At 58, with no savings, I'd be asking how my family would eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my pastor and the women's group first, because they've helped families before. I'd cut the phone, the television package and anything that isn't food, rent and light. And I'd talk to Samir and the children about moving in together to share the costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a flood and I'm standing in my kitchen. Faith tells me not to be afraid, and I try. But a mother is allowed to be afraid for her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you and your husband Samir live if you had to share a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Layla and her husband have a small flat, and it would be tight. My son Yusuf has a room. I'd go there, with Samir, if I had to, and I'd rather it was my idea than theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first, and what do you keep no matter what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm asked what gets cut first, it's the television. Then the second phone. Then the holiday to see my sister. I'd keep paying into the church, though, a small amount, because it feeds other people too.

say: I'd say this is not how a society should treat its **workers**.
I'd ask the church to gather **food and money** for families who lose their jobs.
think: My job is **gone** and I know it, even the shopkeeper visits.
At 58 with no savings, I'd be asking how my **family** would eat.
do: **Go** to my pastor and the women's group first.
**Cut** the phone and television package, keeping only food, rent and light.
**Talk** to Samir and the children about sharing a home.
feel: Like a **flood** while I'm standing in my kitchen, afraid for my family.
S2.quote: A mother is allowed to be afraid for her family.
fieldNote: She expects to lose the job and leans on **church** and family, as her outlook would predict.
Pride is visible: she'd rather propose moving in than be asked.
Keeps a small church donation even in crisis, which says a lot about her values.

steps.text: Go to my pastor and the church women's group for help
Cancel the television package and the second phone
Talk to Samir and the children about sharing one home
Move into Yusuf's spare room with Samir if rent can't be paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we should take seriously. At work I'd ask Mr Ashby to be honest about what happens to the buying desk. At church I'd say we should help each other train, and that those with skills should teach those without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd have a chance but a small one. I'd be 63 and tired, and I'd have to learn things I've avoided all my life. I think I'd manage until about 2030, then it would get hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set aside 40 a week from the first month and I'd learn the order system properly. I'd ask Mr Ashby for a move to the warehouse office, where it's more hands-on checking of deliveries. And I'd look at drawing my pension early at 62 if they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carrying a heavy basket up a long hill is how it feels. I can do it if I take my time, but I can't run. The worry is that the hill gets steeper before I reach the top.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Samir that we should clear the small debts first, the shop card and the loan from his brother. Then every pound we save is ours. He'd agree, though he'd grumble about the loan, which is family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and your husband Samir deal with the small debts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three years of robots coming later matter for Yusuf at the docks, I think. He's got a bit longer to build a trade. For me, the thinking work that goes first is the buying desk, so the extra years are not for me.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** we should take seriously.
I'd tell church friends that those with skills should **teach** those without.
think: I'd have a **chance**, but a small one, aged 63 and tired.
I think I'd manage until **2030**, then it would get hard.
do: **Set** aside 40 a week and learn the order system properly.
**Ask** Mr Ashby for a move to the warehouse office checking deliveries.
feel: Like carrying a **heavy basket** up a long hill; I can do it if I take my time.
S3.quote: Carrying a heavy basket up a long hill is how it feels. I can do it if I take my time, but I can't run.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a plan, but she says the **desk** would still go by about 2030.
Sees the robot delay as helping her son at the docks, not herself.
Wants to clear small family debts first; a careful, practical instinct.

steps.text: Set aside 40 a week from the first month
Learn the order system properly, with a younger colleague's help
Ask Mr Ashby for a move to checking deliveries in the warehouse office
Ask about drawing my pension at 62

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if people don't waste it. At work I'd do my job as usual. At church I'd talk about teaching the young a trade, because a trade gives a person dignity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 by then, so I'd have retired. I'd feel for my grandchildren. I think they will need to know how to do things, and the church and family will matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65 and save every spare pound towards a small pot. I'd teach Layla's children to bake and to keep accounts by hand, just as a bit of heritage. And I'd encourage Yusuf to finish his apprenticeship and perhaps open his own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant, like a story about the future. I'm not scared for myself, but I'd feel anxious for my family. Still, it's easier to sleep when there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the grandchildren to study hard and to learn a skill with their hands. I'd say a person should always be able to look after another person, because that's the one thing a machine will never be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving with your head up look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I can be tired at 65, hand over my ledger, and go home. In the two-year picture I'd be thrown out. Here I can leave with my head up.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** if people don't waste it.
I'd tell church friends to teach the young a **trade**, because it gives dignity.
think: I'd be 68 by then, so I'd have **retired**.
I feel for my **grandchildren**, who will need to know how to do things.
do: **Work** until 65 and save every spare pound.
**Teach** Layla's children to bake and keep accounts by hand.
**Encourage** Yusuf to finish his apprenticeship and open a business.
feel: **Distant**, like a story about the future, easier to sleep with time.
S4.quote: With ten years I can be tired at 65, hand over my ledger, and go home.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her retire before it lands, but **savings** keep her anxious.
Her answer turns to grandchildren and the value of hands-on skills and care.
Strong contrast with the two-year picture, where she'd be 'thrown out'.

steps.text: Save every spare pound into a small pot until I retire at 65
Teach Layla's children to bake and keep a handwritten ledger
Keep working at Ashby & Sons until 65

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because we'd have no time to ready ourselves, and there's no savings in this house. I'd be too old for anybody to take on, and too young to stop. My faith helps, but a church can't pay the rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that work is about more than money. A person who can't work loses something no benefit can replace. I'd ask the people deciding these things to remember that.

headlineQuote: A person who can't work loses something no benefit can replace.
portrait: Amira is 58, a junior buyer at **Ashby & Sons**, a grocery wholesaler, with a plumber husband and two grown children.
She is **resistant** to technology, keeps a handwritten ledger and has never used AI.
She is **traditional**: faith, family and honest work shape her view, and she wants help through apprenticeships, not handouts.
She grows **alarmed** at two years and leans on her church, family and the personal side of the job.
Her biggest fear is losing the **dignity** of work with no savings to fall back on.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because there's no time to get ready and no savings in the house.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** from the firm, apprenticeships for the young, and a bridge until her pension starts.
